propositions.text: Claimants allege they are Convention refugees and persons in need of protection under the Act.
propositions.quote: The claimants, XXXX XXXX and his spouse, XXXX XXXX, are citizens of Haiti and are alleging that they are "Convention refugees" and "persons in need of protection" as defined in section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act).

paragraphs.summary: The claimants allege they are Convention refugees and persons in need of protection under the Act.

propositions.text: Claimants arrived in Brazil in 2011 and allege discrimination there as Haitians.
propositions.quote: The claimants allege that, as Haitians, they faced discrimination there.

paragraphs.summary: The claimants allege discrimination in Brazil as Haitians after arriving in 2011.

propositions.text: Male claimant lived with four men in Brazil, felt good, confirming his bisexual orientation.
propositions.quote: The male claimant states that he felt good in that situation and that that confirmed his bisexual sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant states living with men in Brazil confirmed his bisexual orientation.

propositions.text: Male claimant and spouse were ridiculed for his bisexuality; he was told he deserved to die.
propositions.quote: The principal male claimant states that he was ridiculed by people in his entourage who noticed that he is bisexual. He alleges that his spouse was ridiculed and that he was told that he deserved to die for making her suffer.

paragraphs.summary: The male claimant alleges he and his spouse were ridiculed and threatened due to his bisexuality.

propositions.text: Claimants left Brazil in 2015 for the US due to double discrimination.
propositions.quote: When faced with the double discrimination that they were experiencing, the claimants decided to leave Brazil on XXXX XXXX, 2015, for the United States, where they arrived on XXXX XXXX, 2016.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants left Brazil in 2015 for the US due to discrimination.

propositions.text: Claimants came to Canada in 2017 to claim refugee protection due to US migration policies.
propositions.quote: With the arrival of President Trump and his migration policies, the claimants travelled to Canada to claim refugee protection here on August 11, 2017.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants came to Canada in 2017 to claim refugee protection due to US policies.

propositions.text: Claimants fear returning to Haiti due to mistreatment or death over male claimant's sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: The claimants fear returning to Haiti and being mistreated, or even killed, by the population because of the male claimant's sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants fear returning to Haiti due to male claimant's sexual orientation.

propositions.text: Minister states claimants have been permanent residents of Brazil since 2012, per government lists.
propositions.quote: the Minister states that the claimants have been permanent residents of Brazil since 2012, as their names can be found on lists of people who were given the opportunity to regularize their status by the Brazilian government and to thus receive permanent residence in Brazil.

paragraphs.summary: Minister states claimants have been permanent residents of Brazil since 2012 per government lists.

propositions.text: Minister states permanent resident status in Brazil grants rights similar to Brazilian citizens.
propositions.quote: The Minister states that permanent resident status in Brazil grants the male claimant rights and obligations that are substantially similar to those of Brazilian citizens.

paragraphs.summary: Minister states permanent resident status in Brazil grants rights similar to citizens.

propositions.text: Minister states claimants' permanent resident status in Brazil was valid when they filed in Canada in 2017.
propositions.quote: The Minister states that, when they filed their refugee protection claim in Canada on August 11, 2017, their permanent resident status in Brazil was still valid as two years had not yet passed since they left that country on XXXX XXXX, 2015.

paragraphs.summary: Minister states claimants' permanent resident status in Brazil was valid when filing in Canada in 2017.

propositions.text: Minister argues claimants did not justify abandoning permanent resident status and lack subjective fear of persecution.
propositions.quote: the claimants did not provide reasonable justification for abandoning their permanent resident status and allowing it to expire. Moreover, the Minister states that the claimants' actions, or rather, their lack of efforts, show that they do not have a subjective fear of being persecuted in their country of origin, Haiti.

paragraphs.summary: Minister argues claimants unjustifiably abandoned permanent resident status and lack subjective fear of persecution.

propositions.text: Minister asks RPD to exclude claimants from Convention refugee protection under section 98 of the Act.
propositions.quote: Consequently, the Minister asks the Refugee Protection Division to exclude the claimants from the application of the Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees under section 98 of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Minister asks RPD to exclude claimants from Convention refugee protection under section 98.

propositions.text: Panel finds claimants described in Article 1E of the Convention and thus cannot be Convention refugees or persons in need of protection under section 98.
propositions.quote: The panel determines that the claimants are described in Article 1E of the Convention and that, consequently, they cannot be "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection" under section 98 of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Panel finds claimants fall under Article 1E and cannot be Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.

propositions.text: Claimants established identities by Haitian passports issued in Brazil, photocopies on record.
propositions.quote: The claimants established their identities by means of their Haitian passports issued in Brazil, photocopies of which are on the record.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants established identities by Haitian passports issued in Brazil.

propositions.text: Article 1E excludes persons recognized by third country authorities as having rights and obligations like nationals.
propositions.quote: Article 1E of the Convention reads as follows: This Convention shall not apply to a person who is recognized by the competent authorities of the country in which he has taken residence as having the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of the nationality of that country.

paragraphs.summary: Article 1E excludes persons recognized by third country authorities as having rights like nationals.

propositions.text: Zeng sets criteria for applying Article 1E: status like nationals, loss or failure to acquire status, and balancing factors.
propositions.quote: In Zeng,7 the Federal Court of Appeal sets out the following criteria for determining whether Article 1E of the Convention should apply to a specific case: Considering all relevant factors to the date of the hearing, does the claimant have status, substantially similar to that of its nationals, in the third country? If the answer is yes, the claimant is excluded. If the answer is no, the next question is whether the claimant previously had such status and lost it, or had access to such status and failed to acquire it. If the answer is no, the claimant is not excluded under Article 1E. If the answer is yes, the RPD must consider and balance various factors. These include, but are not limited to, the reason for the loss of status (voluntary or involuntary), whether the claimant could return to the third country, the risk the claimant would face in the home country, Canada's international obligations, and any other relevant facts.

paragraphs.summary: Zeng sets criteria for Article 1E: current status, prior status, loss, and balancing factors.

propositions.text: Female claimant obtained permanent residence in Brazil about one year after arrival in 2011, consistent with Minister's Exhibit M-3.
propositions.quote: The female claimant acknowledged that she obtained permanent residence in Brazil about one year after she arrived in that country on XXXX XXXX, 2011. That is consistent with Exhibit M-3,8 submitted by the Minister, which demonstrates that the female claimant had access to permanent residence in XXXX 2012 according to the publication in the official gazette of Brazil.

propositions.text: Female claimant initially said she had no rights in Brazil but later acknowledged right to work and studied nursing for two years.
propositions.quote: When asked about the rights that she had in Brazil, the female claimant first responded that she did not have any rights in that country. In response to the panel's questions, she acknowledged that she could work. She stated that she had to pay to obtain medical care and to study. The female claimant stated that, nevertheless, she studied nursing sciences for two years.

propositions.text: Female claimant did not allege refusal of care but lacked health insurance.
propositions.quote: She did not allege that she was refused care, but that she did not have any health insurance.

paragraphs.summary: Female claimant obtained permanent residence in Brazil in 2012, acknowledged work rights, studied nursing, lacked health insurance.

propositions.text: Male claimant obtained permanent residence in Brazil in 2012, consistent with Minister's Exhibit M-2.
propositions.quote: With regard to the male claimant, he acknowledged that he obtained permanent residence in Brazil in XXXX or XXXX 2012. That is consistent with Exhibit M-2,9 submitted by the Minister, which demonstrates that the male claimant had access to permanent residence in XXXX 2012 according to the publication in the official gazette of Brazil.

propositions.text: Male claimant stated he had to pay for medical care and lacked medical insurance but was able to work in Brazil.
propositions.quote: When questioned as to the rights granted to him because of his permanent resident status, he stated that, like the female claimant, he did not have access to medical care like Brazilians because, unlike Brazilians, he had to pay to receive care. He also indicated that he did not have medical insurance through his employment. The male claimant was able to work in Brazil.

paragraphs.summary: Male claimant obtained permanent residence in Brazil in 2012, paid for medical care, lacked insurance, but could work.

propositions.text: Permanent residence in Brazil grants rights to return, work, study, and social services including education and health.
propositions.quote: According to the documentary evidence,10 with permanent residence, a foreign national has the right to return to Brazil as a permanent resident, as well as has the right to work, study and have access to social services there. Under the Brazilian Constitution, these social rights include education, health, employment, leisure, security, social security, maternal and child protection, and assistance to the destitute.

propositions.text: Some foreigners face mistreatment by employers withholding insurance or underpaying, but permanent residents have rights they can assert.
propositions.quote: The panel is aware that some foreigners have been mistreated by employers who have tried to withhold medical insurance or underpay employees who are not necessarily aware of all their rights. The fact remains that permanent residents have a certain number of rights in Brazil that they can ask to have respected.

paragraphs.summary: Permanent residents in Brazil have rights to return, work, study, social services, despite some employer mistreatment.

propositions.text: Claimants obtained permanent residence in Brazil in 2012 but lost cards en route to the US.
propositions.quote: Consequently, everything suggests that the claimants obtained permanent residence in Brazil as their names appear on lists of people who were given access to permanent residence in Brazil,11 and the claimants stated that they obtained their permanent residence cards in 2012, but then lost them en route to the United States.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants obtained permanent residence in Brazil in 2012 but lost cards en route to the US.

propositions.text: Claimants had status in Brazil similar to nationals, including free entry, study, work, and social services access.
propositions.quote: The panel concludes, on balance of probabilities, that the claimants had, in Brazil, through their permanent residence, status substantially similar to that of Brazilian nationals, in particular, that of freely entering the country, studying there, working there, and having access to social services there.

propositions.text: Claimants are described in Article 1E of the Convention due to their status.
propositions.quote: They are therefore described in Article 1E of the Convention.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimants had status in Brazil similar to nationals and are described in Article 1E of the Convention.

propositions.text: Relevant date for permanent resident status is hearing date before RPD, per Zeng and Majebi.
propositions.quote: the Court of Appeal clearly established that the relevant date in response to the question of whether a claimant has permanent resident status is that of the hearing before the RPD.

propositions.text: Claimants allege they no longer had permanent resident status at hearing date, over two years after leaving Brazil.
propositions.quote: the claimants alleged that they no longer had permanent resident status on the date of their hearing before the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites case law that relevant date for permanent resident status is hearing date; claimants allege they lost status by then.

propositions.text: Claimants allege they cannot return to Brazil because they left illegally and lost permanent residence after two years.
propositions.quote: The claimants stated that they cannot return to Brazil. They allege that they left Brazil illegally and therefore would be prohibited from returning there. They add that, given that they left Brazil over two years ago, they would have lost their permanent residence.

propositions.text: Claimants did not seek information on maintaining permanent residence, indicating unwillingness to return.
propositions.quote: When questioned if they obtained information as to whether they could maintain their permanent residence despite leaving the country over two years ago, the claimants responded no, indicating that they did not want to return to that country because of what they had experienced there.

propositions.text: Claimants did not demonstrate their situation meets criteria of section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Act.
propositions.quote: The panel, as analyzed below, is of the opinion that the claimants did not demonstrate that their situation in Brazil would meet the criteria of section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants allege they cannot return to Brazil and lost residence; court finds they did not meet legal criteria.

propositions.text: Claimants stated dates of leaving Brazil and arriving in US but have no evidence of travel.
propositions.quote: The claimants stated that they left Brazil on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2015, and arrived in the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2016. They do not have any evidence of their departure from Brazil or of their travel to the United States.

propositions.text: Panel did not believe claimants and found them not credible; claimants failed to establish date of leaving Brazil.
propositions.quote: Since the panel did not believe the claimants with regard to their main allegation, and having found that they are not credible (see below), the panel, without any additional evidence, concludes that the claimants did not establish the date when they left Brazil.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants gave travel dates but no evidence; panel finds them not credible and date unestablished.

propositions.text: Claimants allege leaving without customs stamp prevents return and loss of status is automatic without recourse.
propositions.quote: the claimants did not submit any evidence in support of their allegation that the fact that they left Brazil without going through customs and having their passport stamped would prevent them from returning to that country. The claimants also failed to submit any evidence demonstrating that the loss of permanent resident status in Brazil is automatic and without recourse with Brazilian immigration authorities.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence indicates loss of status after two years absence but does not explain how loss occurs.
propositions.quote: Although the documentary evidence indicates that permanent residents of Brazil lose their status if they are absent from the country for more than two years, it does not indicate how the loss occurs: whether it is automatic, whether there is recourse, whether it occurs when returning to Brazil or while outside the country.

propositions.text: Minister demonstrated claimants had permanent resident status in Brazil, undisputed by claimants.
propositions.quote: once the Minister demonstrated, prima facie, that the claimants had permanent resident status in Brazil-which is not disputed by the claimants

propositions.text: Burden shifted to claimants to prove loss of status at hearing, which they did not do.
propositions.quote: the burden of proof shifted to them and it became their responsibility to demonstrate that they no longer had that status at the time of the hearing, which they did not do.

propositions.text: Claimants did not take steps to prove loss of status, e.g., by contacting Brazilian Embassy.
propositions.quote: They did not even take any steps to demonstrate that they no longer had that status by going to the Embassy of Brazil, for example.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants failed to prove loss of status or inability to return; burden shifted to them and they did not act.

propositions.text: Panel concludes claimants failed to prove loss of permanent resident status and inability to return to Brazil.
propositions.quote: Consequently, the panel concludes that the claimants failed to demonstrate that they lost their permanent resident status in Brazil and that they cannot return there.

paragraphs.summary: Panel concludes claimants failed to prove loss of status and inability to return to Brazil.

propositions.text: Claimants allege they have a fear in Brazil.
propositions.quote: the claimants allege that they have a fear in Brazil.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants allege fear in Brazil.

propositions.text: Panel considered Guideline 9 on sexual orientation and gender identity in IRB proceedings.
propositions.quote: In its assessment of the claimants' credibility, the panel considered Guideline 9: Proceedings Before the IRB Involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression (SOGIE).

paragraphs.summary: Panel considered Guideline 9 on sexual orientation and gender identity in assessing credibility.

propositions.text: Guideline 9 advises members to consider diverse impacts of SOGIE, religion, age, culture, education, and experience on behaviour and testimony.
propositions.quote: The Guideline invites members to consider the fact that people with diverse SOGIE recognize and act on their SOGIE differently. Also, their religion and belief system, their age, their culture, their education and what they experienced in their country of origin can have different impacts on their behaviour and their ability to testify before the IRB.

paragraphs.summary: Guideline 9 advises considering diverse impacts on behaviour and testimony in SOGIE cases.

propositions.text: Members should be prudent before criticizing non-heterosexual claimants for limited explanations of orientation or relationship dynamics.
propositions.quote: Therefore, a member should be prudent before criticizing a claimant with an orientation other than heterosexual, as in this case, for only being able to state that it is natural and he could not help himself when asked why, when he decided to marry his spouse, he continued his relationship with a man, without providing further explanations demonstrating a degree of reflection with regard to the situation he is in.

propositions.text: It is delicate to criticize the female claimant for inability to explain staying with spouse despite his affair with a man, given couple dynamics and cultural taboos.
propositions.quote: Similarly, it would be a delicate matter to criticize the female claimant for her inability to explain, in a thoughtful manner, how and why, after learning that her spouse was having a relationship with a man, she decided to stay with him and continue their relationship, aside from stating that he is a good man to her, that she loves him and that she understood that it is natural for him to be who he is. Although the panel was not satisfied with their explications, it also understands that couples have different dynamics and rationales. The panel also considered that it is taboo to discuss non-heterosexual relations in Haitian culture.

paragraphs.summary: Guideline advises prudence in criticizing claimants' explanations of orientation and relationship, considering culture and dynamics.

propositions.text: Panel found claimants not credible due to contradictions and omissions in their allegations.
propositions.quote: That said, the panel still found that the claimants were not credible because of contradictions and omissions at the heart of their allegations, as illustrated below.

paragraphs.summary: Panel found claimants not credible due to contradictions and omissions.

propositions.text: Male claimant tried to intervene during wife's testimony and told his story instead of answering questions, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: the male claimant, on a number of occasions, wanted to intervene during the testimony of his wife, who was questioned first, in order to provide details in her place. Moreover, when he was questioned in turn, the male claimant, rather than responding to the panel's questions, tried, on a number of occasions, to tell his story. These two factors undermine their credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Male claimant's conduct during testimony undermined claimants' credibility.

propositions.text: Female claimant gave inconsistent dates for when problems began, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: The female claimant initially stated that her problems in Brazil began in 2014. When the panel asked her to be more specific, she stated that she married the male claimant on XXXX XXXX, 2014, and that the problems began two or three months later. When confronted by the panel regarding the fact that that meant that the problems began in January or February 2015, rather than in 2014, the female claimant agreed. The female claimant did not know when her problems began, which undermines her credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Female claimant gave inconsistent dates for problems' start, undermining credibility.

propositions.text: Female claimant made contradictory statements about staying with spouse despite his affairs, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: The female claimant also made contradictory statements when the panel tried to understand through its questions what motivated her to stay with the male claimant after she discovered that he was having an affair with a man. When the panel asked her if she would have stayed with the male claimant if he had had affairs with women during their marriage, she responded no. To the same question, that is, if she would be willing to stay with the male claimant if he had affairs with men, she responded that, normally, it would not sit well with her, but that she loved him too much. Then, the panel asked her to confirm that if her spouse had affairs with women, she would leave him, but not if he had affairs with men, she stated then that even if he were cheating on her with women, she would not leave him. It is up to the female claimant to decide whether she would stay with her spouse based on the situation before her. However, the female claimant cannot state that she would leave her spouse and then respond that she would not leave him based on the panel's questions. These adjustments undermine her credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Female claimant contradicted herself about staying with spouse despite affairs, undermining credibility.

propositions.text: Male claimant contradicted himself on when he realized attraction to men versus when relationship began, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: With regard to the male claimant, he stated that he realized that he was attracted to men in late 2012. He explained that he lived with four men with whom he did everything. He stated that he began having feelings for XXXX XXXX XXXX and that, in 2012, he realized that he was attracted to men. When questioned as to when his relationship with XXXX began, he responded that it began about four months after he started living with the four men in XXXX 2011. The male claimant confirmed that his relationship with XXXX began in XXXX 2011 when they kissed. When the panel asked him how he reacted at that time, the male claimant explained that he felt that something was telling him that he was attracted to XXXX. He explained that they then had intimate relations for the first time. The male claimant was then confronted with his previous statement that he realized that he was attracted to men in late 2012, whereas he was now claiming that he began his relationship with XXXX in XXXX 2011. The claimant then stated that, in XXXX 2011, he experienced love at first sight but that it was not until 2012 that he realized that it was natural. When the panel pointed out to him that the initial question was not when he had accepted his attraction to men as being something natural, but rather, when he realized that he was attracted to men, and that, in late 2012, he had already been in a relationship with XXXX for over a year, the male claimant could only respond that he had made a mistake.

paragraphs.summary: Male claimant contradicted himself on timing of attraction and relationship, undermining credibility.

propositions.text: Male claimant failed to mention a key relationship in his account, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: The male claimant was also confronted with the fact that he failed to mention his relationship with XXXX in his account, a relationship that allegedly lasted nearly four years.

propositions.text: Male claimant's explanations for omission evolved and were inconsistent, further undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: The male claimant's explanations regarding that omission evolved as the panel asked its questions. He first explained that he had not wanted to upset his spouse, stated that his account was merely a summary, alleged that he had submitted documents in support of his allegations, then stated that his relationships with men can be inferred.

propositions.text: Omission of a central relationship in the refugee claim greatly undermines male claimant's credibility.
propositions.quote: Such an omission on a central aspect of his refugee protection claim, that is, that he had had a four-year relationship with a man in Brazil, as well as two others in the United States, and then in Canada, greatly undermines his credibility in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: Male claimant omitted key relationship in claim and gave inconsistent explanations, undermining credibility.

propositions.text: Male claimant contradicted himself about timing of problems before marriage, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: When the panel asked him if he had had problems before his marriage in XXXX 2014, he responded that, maybe, people did not know about his relationship with XXXX or his sexual orientation. Shortly afterward, when the panel was surprised at the fact that he was able to maintain a relationship with XXXX for nearly three years without any problems, but that, two or three months after his wedding, problems arose all of a sudden, the male claimant changed his testimony and responded that he had already been the victim of insults before his wedding. When the panel confronted him with his previous testimony, which was completely contrary, the claimant stated that he had misunderstood the question and believed that the panel was asking him to identify the problems he had while he was married to the female claimant.

paragraphs.summary: Male claimant contradicted himself on timing of problems before marriage, undermining credibility.

propositions.text: Male claimant did not provide evidence of precautions despite alleged fear, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: Despite the insults and threats that he allegedly received in the street, the male claimant did not provide evidence of any precautions. That does not demonstrate that the male claimant has a subjective fear, and it undermines his credibility in that it is implausible that a person who alleges they fear for their physical safety would not try to minimize his risks.

paragraphs.summary: Male claimant's failure to show precautions despite fear undermines credibility.

propositions.text: Male claimant submitted Exhibit C-3 of WhatsApp messages with three men he had relationships with.
propositions.quote: The male claimant submitted Exhibit C-3 titled Email exchanges between XXXX and his boyfriend. When questioned, the male claimant stated that it was a message exchange on WhatsApp between him and three men with whom he had had a relationship: XXXX XXXX XXXX in Brazil, XXXX XXXX in the United States and XXXX XXXX in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Male claimant submitted WhatsApp message exhibit with three men he had relationships with.

propositions.text: Many messages in Exhibit C-3 are untranslated Creole, so panel cannot understand most content.
propositions.quote: First, the panel would like to point out that a number of passages in these exchanges are in Creole and were not translated, thereby violating subrule 32(1). Consequently, and considering the nature of the document, the panel does not understand the majority of the content of Exhibit C-3.

propositions.text: All messages dated after claimants arrived in Canada and filed refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The panel also notes that all the messages with these three men are dated between XXXX 2017 and XXXX 2018, that is, following the claimants' arrival in Canada and their refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: Panel notes untranslated Creole in messages and that all messages postdate claimants' arrival in Canada.

propositions.text: The claimant was confronted with inconsistent spellings of names in messages in Exhibit C-3.
propositions.quote: The male claimant was then confronted with the fact that the spelling of the names of those men changes from one message to the next.

propositions.text: Claimant explained misspellings as sender errors, but messaging apps automatically identify sender names.
propositions.quote: The male claimant then tried to explain that it was the person who sent the message who misspelled his name. However, in message applications like WhatsApp or Messenger, or even in texts, the person does not write their name before every message that he or she sends.

propositions.text: Claimant's explanation about name misspellings is unsatisfactory.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the claimant's response is not satisfactory.

propositions.text: Claimant said name changes might have happened when he changed phones and entered info anew.
propositions.quote: When confronted with this, he stated that it might have happened when he changed telephones and entered XXXX information in his new telephone.

propositions.text: Panel pointed out two messages sent one after another with different spellings, undermining claimant's explanation.
propositions.quote: The panel then pointed out to him that, still on page 5 of C-3, XXXX sent him two messages one after another on XXXX XXXX at 5:08 p.m. with two different spellings: XXXX and XXXX.

propositions.text: Claimant's explanation about changing phones within the same minute does not hold water.
propositions.quote: Given that these two messages were sent within a very short time frame on the same day, yet again, the male claimant's explanation does not hold water because he would not have been able to change his cellular telephone and information within that same minute.

propositions.text: Claimant said his phone stopped working on Wi-Fi and he had to change phones one night.
propositions.quote: Consequently, the claimant tried to explain that, one night, the cellular telephone that he was using on Wi-Fi stopped working and that he had to change his cellular telephone.

propositions.text: Panel confronted claimant with two messages sent one minute apart with different spellings; claimant could not explain.
propositions.quote: The panel confronted him with the two messages dated XXXX XXXX (at the top of page 5 of Exhibit C-3): one at 7:27 p.m. "XXXX" and another at 7:28 p.m. "XXXX." The male claimant stated that he could not explain it.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant's explanations for inconsistent name spellings in messages unsatisfactory and unconvincing.

propositions.text: Panel noted similar name spelling problems with messages from another person in Exhibit C-3.
propositions.quote: The panel pointed out to the male claimant that the same type of problem occurred with the messages from XXXX XXXX, whose name appears in turn as XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX on the messages appearing on pages 6 and 7 of Exhibit C-3.

propositions.text: Claimant explained he asked a friend to send messages to lawyer to hide from spouse.
propositions.quote: The claimant tried to then explain that, when he sent the copy of those messages to his lawyer to disclose them, he did not want his spouse to know and consequently asked a friend to do it for him.

propositions.text: Claimant's explanation does not explain the spelling differences in the document.
propositions.quote: That does not explain the spelling differences in the names appearing in that document.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant's explanation for name spelling differences in messages sent by a friend does not explain the inconsistencies.

propositions.text: Panel does not grant probative value to Exhibit C-3 and considers it fabricated by claimant.
propositions.quote: Consequently, the panel does not grant any probative value to Exhibit C-3, and is rather of the opinion that it is a fabrication by the male claimant.

propositions.text: Claimant's changing explanations undermine his credibility severely.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the male claimant's adjustment of his explanations in line with the panel's reactions to his responses severely undermines his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Exhibit C-3 fabricated and the claimant's credibility severely undermined by his changing explanations.

propositions.text: Panel finds claimants not credible and disbelieves their allegations about male claimant's bisexuality and related persecution fears in Brazil and Haiti.
propositions.quote: For all these reasons, the panel finds that the claimants are not credible and therefore does not believe their allegations that the male claimant is bisexual, that he had had intimate relations with men or that he could be perceived as bisexual, and that he would consequently face persecution, both in Brazil and in Haiti, within the meaning of the Convention.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimants not credible and disbelieves their allegations about bisexuality and persecution fears.

propositions.text: Claimants allege fear of returning to Brazil due to discrimination against Haitians and lack of government protection.
propositions.quote: The claimants allege that they fear returning to Brazil because Brazilians discriminate against Haitians there and the government would not do anything to protect them.

propositions.text: Claimants also allege fear of returning due to male claimant's sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: The claimants also allege that they fear returning there because of the male claimant's sexual orientation.

propositions.text: Panel has already ruled on sexual orientation topic and will now decide on Haitians' situation in Brazil.
propositions.quote: Since the panel has already ruled on that topic, it will now decide on the situation of Haitians in Brazil.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants allege fear of returning to Brazil due to discrimination and sexual orientation; panel will now consider Haitians' situation in Brazil.

propositions.text: Claimants state discrimination in Brazil in employment, daily life, and access to rights as permanent residents.
propositions.quote: The claimants stated that they were discriminated against in Brazil in relation to employment, in everyday life while taking the bus and with regard to access to rights to which they are entitled as permanent residents of Brazil.

propositions.text: Female claimant states Brazilians pushed her at bus and Brazilians went before Haitians at appointments and stores.
propositions.quote: The female claimant stated that, when she waited for the bus, Brazilians pushed her so that they could enter before her and that Brazilians went before Haitians at appointments with professionals or in stores.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants allege discrimination in Brazil in employment, daily life, and access to rights; female claimant describes being pushed at bus and Brazilians cutting ahead.

propositions.text: Some foreigners faced employer abuse like withholding medical insurance or underpayment in Brazil.
propositions.quote: As the panel stated above, some foreigners have had to deal with abuse by employers who have tried withholding medical insurance or underpaying employees who were not necessarily aware of all their rights.

propositions.text: Permanent residents in Brazil have rights they can demand to be respected.
propositions.quote: The fact remains that permanent residents have a certain number of rights in Brazil that they can demand to have respected.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes some foreigners faced employer abuse but permanent residents have rights they can demand in Brazil.

propositions.text: Economic and social situation in Brazil deteriorated after Olympics and World Cup, reducing construction jobs.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the panel is aware that the economic and social situation has deteriorated in Brazil following the Olympic Games and the World Cup, which created numerous construction jobs that no longer exist today.

propositions.text: Decreased employment and racism cause hesitation to hire foreigners or rent to them if they have little means.
propositions.quote: The panel is aware that, with a decrease in employment levels, it would be more difficult to find work and that a degree of racism exists in a difficult economic context, which results in hesitation to hire a foreigner or rent him or her housing when that same foreigner has little economic means available.

propositions.text: Accumulated difficulties do not amount to persecution.
propositions.quote: Still, even through accumulation, that does not amount to persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes economic decline and racism in Brazil but finds these hardships do not amount to persecution.

propositions.text: Brazil has high murder rates and serious crime and police violence problems; 85,000 Haitians arrived since 2012.
propositions.quote: With regard to crime, the evidence indicates that Brazil, where 85,000 Haitians have arrived since 2012,21 has one of the highest murder rates in the world and that crime and police violence are serious problems in Brazilian cities.

propositions.text: Special Rapporteur shocked by violence in Brazil, noting racial dimension and police killings disproportionately affecting Afro-Brazilian youth.
propositions.quote: The Special Rapporteur was shocked to learn about the levels of violence in Brazil. Regrettably this violence has a clear racial dimension. Of the 56,000 homicides that occur each year, 30,000 victims are between 15 and 29 years old, of which 77 per cent are Afro- Brazilian male youth. What is disconcerting is that a significant number are perpetrated by the State, often through the apparatus of the military police.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Brazil's high murder rates and racialized police violence disproportionately affecting Afro-Brazilian youth.

propositions.text: Male claimant did not state fear of police, state apparatus, gangs, or militias in Brazil.
propositions.quote: That said, the panel notes that the male claimant did not, at any time, state that he fears the actions of the police and the state apparatus, or gangs or other militias.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the male claimant did not express fear of police or gangs in Brazil.

propositions.text: Brazil is one of the most violent countries with homicide rate 27.1 per 100,000 in 2011; violence linked to organized crime and drug trafficking.
propositions.quote: Overall, Brazil is one of the most violent countries in the world, with a homicide rate of 27.1 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2011. As in other parts of Southern and Central America, a large part of this violence and criminality can be linked to organized crime groups participating in drug trafficking.

propositions.text: Murder victims often young black men from poor urban areas recruited by drug gangs.
propositions.quote: The murder victims are frequently young black men from poor urban areas who are constantly recruited by drug gangs.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites evidence that Brazil's violence is linked to organized crime, affecting young black men from poor areas.

propositions.text: Black youth homicides mainly due to socio-economic factors and drug cartel recruitment, not persecution based on race or Haitian origin.
propositions.quote: Consequently, while is true that the black youth are overrepresented in terms of homicide, this excerpt indicates that the victims are killed mainly because of a negative socio-economic context, which pushes them to be recruited by drug cartels in the poorest urban areas, and not because of persecution targeting black people or people of Haitian origin.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds black youth homicides in Brazil result from socio-economic factors, not persecution based on race or origin.

propositions.text: Claimants failed to show serious possibility of persecution or risk under subsection 97(1) if returned to Brazil.
propositions.quote: For all these reasons, the panel concludes that the claimants failed to demonstrate that, if they returned to Brazil, they would face a serious possibility of persecution by reason of their ethnicity or another ground, or that, on a balance of probabilities, they would be subjected to a danger of torture, a risk of cruel or unusual treatment or punishment or a risk to their lives under subsection 97(1) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimants failed to prove serious risk of persecution or harm if returned to Brazil.

propositions.text: Claimants excluded from definition of Convention refugee and person in need of protection under section 98 of the Act.
propositions.quote: Given the above analysis to the effect that the claimants failed to demonstrate that, in Brazil, they would face persecution or a risk within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the Act, the panel determines that the claimants are excluded from the definition of "Convention refugee" and "person in need of protection" under section 98 of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court excludes claimants from refugee and protection definitions under section 98 of the Act.

propositions.text: Federal Court in Zhong held that voluntary lapse of status without reasonable justification can lead to exclusion under Article 1(E) of the Convention.
propositions.quote: The Board considered the Applicants' status in Ecuador at the time they made their claim for refugee protection in Canada, and their status in Ecuador at the time of the hearing... Consequently, I am unable to find that the Board erred in concluding that the Applicants were excluded under Article 1(E) of the Convention.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Federal Court in Zhong on exclusion for voluntary lapse of status without reasonable justification.

propositions.text: Claimants allege they do not want to return to Brazil due to double persecution for Haitian origin and male claimant's bisexuality.
propositions.quote: Similar to that decision, the claimants in the case at hand did not take any steps to retain their status in Brazil. Rather, they allege that they do not want to return to Brazil, stating that they would be doubly persecuted, that is, by reason of their Haitian origin and the male claimant's bisexuality.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants allege fear of double persecution in Brazil due to Haitian origin and bisexuality, explaining their inaction on status.

propositions.text: Panel found claimants not credible on bisexuality and failed to show persecution in Haiti or Brazil on that basis.
propositions.quote: The panel, having found that the claimants are not credible in their allegations that the male claimant is bisexual and, therefore, that they failed to demonstrate that they would face persecution both in Haiti and Brazil in that regard; having concluded that the claimants failed to demonstrate that they would face persecution in Brazil based on the colour of their skin or their Haitian origin; and because the claimants did not allege any other fear of persecution or risk within the meaning of subsection 97(1), either in Brazil or in Haiti, concludes that the fears cited by the claimants to explain their lack of efforts in terms of maintaining or renewing their status as permanent residents of Brazil are not reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimants not credible on bisexuality and concludes their fears justifying status lapse are unreasonable.

propositions.text: Claimants voluntarily let permanent resident status expire without reasonable excuse and failed to show persecution or risk in Haiti or Brazil.
propositions.quote: Consequently, taking into consideration the various factors to be weighed according to Zeng,27 that is, that the claimants allegedly voluntarily let their permanent resident status expire by leaving Brazil and their subsequent inaction in terms of maintaining their status, without a reasonable excuse; that the claimants did not demonstrate that they could not return to Brazil; that the claimants did not demonstrate that they would face persecution or a risk within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the Act, both in their country of origin, Haiti, and in their country of permanent residence, Brazil; that the claimants, without providing any evidence, allegedly applied for asylum in the United States, but abandoned their application to come and claim protection in Canada; and that the panel concluded that the claimants have neither a fear nor a risk within the meaning of the Act, either in Haiti or Brazil, excluding them does not violate Canada's international obligations.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimants voluntarily let status expire without excuse and failed to show persecution or risk in Haiti or Brazil.

propositions.text: Claimants are described in Article 1E of the Convention and excluded from refugee and protection definitions under section 98 of the Act.
propositions.quote: For all these reasons, taking into consideration all aspects of their refugee protection claim, the panel determines that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimants are described in Article 1E of the Convention and are excluded from the definition of "Convention refugee" and "person in need of protection" under section 98 of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimants are excluded under Article 1E and section 98 of the Act.

propositions.text: Even if not excluded, claimants failed to show serious possibility of persecution or risk in Haiti.
propositions.quote: Finally, even if the panel had not concluded that the claimants are excluded, given the above analysis of the claimants' credibility regarding their allegation that the male claimant is bisexual, and given that they did not allege any other fear of returning to Haiti, the panel would have concluded that the claimants failed to demonstrate that there is a serious possibility that they would be persecuted in Haiti on one of the Convention grounds or that, on a balance of probabilities, they would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to their lives, or a risk of cruel or unusual treatment or punishment if they returned.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that even if not excluded, claimants failed to prove serious risk of persecution or harm in Haiti.

propositions.text: Claimants cannot be Convention refugees or persons in need of protection under section 98 due to Article 1E and permanent residence in Brazil
propositions.quote: the claimants, XXXX XXXX and his spouse, XXXX XXXX XXXX cannot be "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection" under section 98 of the Act because they are described in Article 1E of the Convention given their permanent residence in Brazil.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimants cannot be Convention refugees or persons in need of protection due to Article 1E and their permanent residence in Brazil.

propositions.text: Refugee protection claim is rejected
propositions.quote: Consequently, their refugee protection claim is rejected.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the refugee protection claim.
